title: Aeronautic Development Corp. (Apr 2018 TCC) SR&ED Case
subject: FCA appeal reviewing TCC's finding on CCPC status and de facto control affecting enhanced refundable SR&ED ITCs.
summary: Aeronautic Development Corporation v. Her Majesty the Queen (2018 FCA 67, affirming 2017 TCC 39) confirms that a Canadian SR&ED claimant controlled in fact by a non-resident is not a CCPC. Because a non-arm's length development agreement gave Seawind Corp. and Mr. Silva de facto control, ADC lost enhanced 35% refundable investment tax credits for 2009 to 2011.
metaDescription: Analyze the April 2018 Tax Court of Canada ruling for Aeronautic Development Corp. on Canadian SR&ED tax credit documentation.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary and Case Background
Procedural Posture and Identification of the Ruling

The litigation in Aeronautic Development Corporation v. Her Majesty the Queen represents watershed trial and appellate jurisprudence within Canadian tax law governing the eligibility of corporations for enhanced refundable Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Investment Tax Credits (ITCs). The April 4, 2018 ruling—bearing neutral citation 2018 FCA 67 (Docket A-121-17)—is the unanimous judgment of the Federal Court of Appeal (per Gleason J.A., with Nadon and Boivin JJ.A. concurring) affirming the trial decision of the Tax Court of Canada rendered by Justice Robert J. Hogan in 2017 TCC 39, [2017] 4 C.T.C. 2140 (judgment dated March 13, 2017), although the Federal Court of Appeal expressly disagreed with aspects of the Tax Court's reasoning. Following the Federal Court of Appeal's dismissal of the taxpayer's appeal on April 4, 2018, the taxpayer filed an application for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada on June 1, 2018 (Docket 38132), which was dismissed with costs on March 7, 2019, leaving the Federal Court of Appeal's judgment—including its corrections to Justice Hogan's reasoning on the scope of subsection 256(5.1)—as the final appellate word on the matter.
The Taxpayer's Claim and Operational Context

The appellant, Aeronautic Development Corporation (ADC), was a Canadian corporation incorporated under the laws of Nova Scotia in April 2009 at the instance of Mr. Richard Silva, operating out of a hangar at the airport in St-Jean-sur-Richelieu, Quebec, that functioned as a specialized aerospace development and certification entity. ADC was engaged under a development agreement by Seawind Corp., a U.S. corporation controlled by Mr. Silva (an American citizen and, at all material times, an American resident), to complete the prototyping and certification of the "Seawind" amphibious aircraft on a cost-plus basis; between 2009 and 2011, Seawind Corp. was ADC's sole client (contemporaneous industry reporting also describes flight testing of the Seawind conducted with assistance from the National Research Council of Canada (NRC)).

In filing its T2 corporate income tax returns and Form T661 SR&ED claims for the 2009, 2010, and 2011 taxation years, ADC claimed enhanced refundable SR&ED ITCs on its qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Quebec. ADC predicated its entitlement to the enhanced 35% refundable ITC rate on the assertion that it was, during the 2009 to 2011 taxation years (it being common ground that ADC was not a CCPC prior to August 2009, when Seawind Corp. held all of its issued shares), a "Canadian-controlled private corporation" (CCPC) pursuant to subsection 125(7) of the Canadian Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "ITA"). Seawind Corp. was initially ADC's sole shareholder; approximately four months after the development agreement was signed (in August 2009), ADC issued additional common shares to one of its employees and to Canadian corporations controlled by three of its employees, reducing Seawind Corp.'s holding to 46% of the issued voting common shares, while Seawind Corp. remained ADC's sole client and source of financing.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

Upon audit and reassessment, the Minister of National Revenue (the "Minister"), administered through the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), disallowed ADC's claim for refundable SR&ED ITCs for the 2009, 2010, and 2011 taxation years. The Minister challenged ADC's CCPC status on the basis of two interrelated statutory questions under the ITA. First, under subsections 125(7) and 256(5.1) of the ITA, the Minister assessed ADC on the basis that it was controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever (de facto control), by a non-resident person—namely Mr. Silva, acting directly and through Seawind Corp.—throughout the relevant taxation years. Second, although the Minister's Reply did not specifically outline the position that ADC was not dealing at arm's length with Mr. Silva and Seawind Corp., the arm's length question under paragraph 251(1)(c) of the ITA became a live issue at trial because ADC relied on the exception in subsection 256(5.1) for influence derived from a supply or similar agreement with an arm's length controller, and ADC's counsel made oral submissions on that issue, largely in response to questions from the Tax Court judge. Notably, the Reply merely listed the relevant ITA provisions and briefly summarized the Minister's position; subsection 152(9) of the ITA was not relied on, and the procedural dispute that later arose concerned whether the Tax Court could consider the unpleaded arm's length issue at all.
Governing Statutory Framework Under the Canadian Income Tax Act

In Canadian federal tax law, eligibility for SR&ED tax incentives is bifurcated between a technical and financial expenditure qualification regime and a corporate status regime that governs the rate and refundability of the resulting tax credits. Subsection 248(1) of the ITA defines "scientific research and experimental development" as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis, encompassing basic research, applied research, and experimental development undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement. Section 37 of the ITA permits a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada to deduct current SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada and sets out the expenditure pool mechanics, under which qualified expenditures are reduced by government assistance, non-government assistance, or prescribed contract payments.

The rate and cash refundability of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits are governed by subsections 127(9), 127(10.1), and 127.1(1) of the ITA. While a general Canadian corporation is limited to a non-refundable basic federal SR&ED ITC that can only be applied to offset Part I federal income tax otherwise payable, a qualifying corporation that maintains status as a CCPC throughout the taxation year is eligible under subsection 127(10.1) for an enhanced 35% ITC rate on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to its annual expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.2), which, for the taxation years at issue, was reduced by reference to the prior-year taxable income and taxable capital of the corporation and its associated corporations. Crucially, under section 127.1, a qualifying CCPC is entitled to receive up to 100% of those enhanced ITCs on current expenditures as an immediate cash refund, even when operating in a loss position with nil Part I tax payable.

Entitlement to CCPC status hinges on subsection 125(7) of the ITA, which defines a CCPC as a private corporation that is a Canadian corporation other than a corporation controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons, by one or more public corporations, or by any combination thereof. The statutory expression "controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever" is defined in subsection 256(5.1) to capture de facto control (control in fact), which exists where a controller has any direct or indirect influence that, if exercised, would result in control in fact of the corporation. Under the appellate standard articulated by the Federal Court of Appeal in Silicon Graphics Ltd. v. The Queen, 2002 DTC 7112 (2002 FCA 260), and reaffirmed in McGillivray Restaurant Ltd. v. The Queen, 2016 DTC 5048 (2016 FCA 99), for taxation years beginning prior to March 22, 2017, a finding of de facto control required that the alleged controller possess a legally enforceable right and ability to effect a change to the board of directors or its powers, or to exercise influence over the shareholder or shareholders who have that right and ability. For taxation years beginning after March 21, 2017, Parliament enacted subsection 256(5.11) of the ITA to explicitly broaden the judicial inquiry, mandating that courts take all relevant operational, contractual, and economic factors into consideration, and specifying that the determination is not limited to whether the taxpayer has a legally enforceable right or ability to effect a change in the board of directors or its powers, or to exercise influence over shareholders who have that right or ability.

Complementing the corporate control regime is paragraph 251(1)(c) of the ITA, under which it is a question of fact whether persons not related to each other are at a particular time dealing with each other at arm's length. In this case, the arm's length question arose under the exception in subsection 256(5.1), which provides that a corporation is not considered controlled by a controller by reason only of a franchise, licence, lease, distribution, supply or management agreement (or similar agreement or arrangement) the main purpose of which is to govern the relationship between the corporation and the controller regarding the manner in which a business carried on by the corporation is to be conducted—but only where the corporation and the controller are dealing with each other at arm's length.
The Court's Final Holding

Both the Tax Court of Canada (2017 TCC 39) and the Federal Court of Appeal (2018 FCA 67) ruled against Aeronautic Development Corporation and dismissed its appeals in their entirety. Justice Hogan at trial found that, despite the issuance of a majority of the voting shares to ADC's employees and their Canadian corporations, Seawind Corp. and Mr. Silva had direct or indirect influence that, if exercised, would result in control in fact of ADC from August 2009 to December 31, 2011 within the meaning of subsection 256(5.1) of the ITA, and that the supply-agreement exception did not apply because ADC was not dealing at arm's length with them. The Federal Court of Appeal held that the Tax Court erred in law in two respects—by effectively applying an operational-control test (relying on factors such as ADC's financial position, the other shareholders' dependence on ADC's viability, and Mr. Silva's newsletters) contrary to McGillivray Restaurant, and by treating the fact that ADC and Seawind Corp. were related before August 2009 as relevant—but found these errors immaterial: the development agreement was a legally enforceable arrangement capable of establishing de facto control, it was a supply agreement, and the Tax Court made no reviewable error in finding that ADC, Mr. Silva and Seawind Corp. were not dealing at arm's length during the relevant period, so the exception in subsection 256(5.1) was unavailable. Consequently, ADC was not a CCPC during its 2009, 2010, and 2011 taxation years and was disqualified from claiming refundable SR&ED Investment Tax Credits.
2. Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

The total disqualification of Aeronautic Development Corporation's refundable SR&ED claims resulted from a convergence of structural corporate defects, a legally enforceable development (supply) agreement dictated by the non-resident principal, non-arm's length dealings between ADC and Seawind Corp./Mr. Silva, and near-total economic dependence on a single non-resident client. A rigorous legal and technical dissection of the ruling reveals five interconnected failures that frequently undermine cross-border Canadian R&D structures.
Failure 1: Artificial Share Capital Engineering and Non-Resident De Facto Control Under Subsections 125(7) and 256(5.1)

A recurring tax-planning failure in cross-border Canadian R&D ventures occurs when a foreign founder or parent corporation establishes a Canadian R&D subsidiary and attempts to access the 35% refundable CCPC SR&ED ITC rate simply by placing 50% or more of the common voting shares in the hands of Canadian residents, such as local managers, engineers, or professional advisors. Under traditional de jure control jurisprudence established by the Supreme Court of Canada in Duha Printers (Western) Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 6334 ([1998] 1 S.C.R. 795), legal control rests with the owner of such a number of shares as carries with it the right to a majority of the votes in the election of the board of directors, subject only to the corporate constating documents and any unanimous shareholder agreement.

However, the CCPC definition in subsection 125(7) of the ITA expressly expands the control test beyond de jure voting power through the words "controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever," thereby importing the de facto control regime of subsection 256(5.1). In Aeronautic Development Corporation, ADC relied heavily on the Federal Court of Appeal's jurisprudence, principally McGillivray Restaurant (2016 DTC 5048) (with Silicon Graphics (2002 DTC 7112) also invoked in its subsequent leave application), arguing that operational dependency or economic influence exercised by Mr. Silva and Seawind Corp. could not legally constitute de facto control, that the development agreement was the only legal basis on which de facto control could be grounded, and that this agreement was a supply agreement falling within the exception in subsection 256(5.1).

Justice Gleason (2018 FCA 67) agreed with ADC that Justice Hogan (2017 TCC 39) had erred by effectively applying an operational-control test—asking whether the controller could affect the economic interest of the voting shareholders so as to impose his will on them—but nonetheless rejected ADC's defence because, as ADC conceded, the development agreement was itself a legally enforceable arrangement capable of establishing de facto control under subsection 256(5.1). Under that agreement, whose terms were set by Mr. Silva, all intellectual property rights were to belong to Mr. Silva and Seawind Corp., ADC's expenses (net of refundable ITCs) were reimbursed by Seawind Corp., ADC was to remit the refundable ITCs it received to Seawind Corp., equipment funded by Seawind Corp. was to be transferred to it on completion, and the 5% mark-up payable to ADC was never paid at Mr. Silva's direction; the Tax Court also noted that ADC had nominal share capital and offered no potential for earnings growth to justify its employees' investment. Because ADC, Mr. Silva and Seawind Corp. were not dealing at arm's length, the supply-agreement exception could not shield ADC, and the finding that ADC was controlled in fact by non-residents under subsection 256(5.1) stood.

Furthermore, from a second- and third-order advisory perspective, Aeronautic Development Corporation bridges the gap between pre-2017 jurisprudence and the modern statutory regime under subsection 256(5.11), which applies to taxation years commencing after March 21, 2017. Enacted specifically to overturn the narrow interpretation of McGillivray Restaurant, subsection 256(5.11) mandates that the determination of de facto control must take all relevant factors into consideration and is expressly not limited to whether the taxpayer has a legally enforceable right or ability to effect a change in the board of directors or to exercise influence over shareholders who have that right. Thus, while ADC failed even under the stricter McGillivray Restaurant standard because its legally enforceable development agreement with a non-arm's length non-resident controller conferred the requisite influence, contemporary SR&ED claimants face an even broader statutory net in which economic, operational, and contractual dominance by a non-resident can be taken into account under subsection 256(5.1) by virtue of subsection 256(5.11).
Failure 2: Violation of the Factual Arm's Length Requirement Under Paragraph 251(1)(c)

Closely intertwined with the de facto control analysis was ADC's failure to establish that ADC itself—rather than its shareholders—was dealing at arm's length, during the period in which de facto control was alleged to exist, with Mr. Silva and Seawind Corp. Under Canadian tax principles governing paragraph 251(1)(c) of the ITA, determining whether unrelated parties deal with each other at arm's length requires a holistic factual examination of whether there is a common mind that directs the bargaining for both parties to a transaction, whether the parties are acting in concert without separate economic interests, and whether one party exercises de facto control or overbearing influence over the other.

In 2017 TCC 39, Justice Hogan concluded that the requirement for arm's length dealings was wholly unsatisfied. The Tax Court relied on Mr. Silva's role in setting the terms of the development agreement, ADC's failure to seek renegotiation after the initial 15-month term expired despite operating at a deficit, Mr. Silva's unilateral decision not to pay the 5% mark-up the agreement called for, and ADC's rent-free occupation, without a lease, of a hangar leased by another corporation controlled by Mr. Silva. The Federal Court of Appeal held that these factors (other than the two companies' related status before August 2009) provided more than ample basis for the finding, stressing that, given ADC's near-total economic dependence on Seawind Corp., Mr. Silva's ability to dictate—and to disregard—the terms of the agreement was highly relevant, and that it would be difficult to imagine a stronger indicator of a non-arm's length relationship than operating out of another's facility for free, without a lease. Where a corporation is economically captive to a non-resident principal who dictates, and can unilaterally override, the terms of their contractual relationship, Canadian courts look past the form of the agreement and find factual non-arm's length dealings under paragraph 251(1)(c), which in turn removes the protection of the commercial-agreement exception in subsection 256(5.1).
Failure 3: Single-Client Captive R&D Contracting, Economic Subservience, and Funded Research Traps

The commercial relationship between Seawind Corp. and ADC exemplified a classic "captive R&D service provider" trap. ADC possessed no diversified customer base, no independent revenue stream, and no autonomous commercialization strategy; between 2009 and 2011 its sole client was Seawind Corp., under a development agreement to complete the prototyping and certification of the Seawind aircraft on a cost-plus basis. This single-client contractual architecture created acute legal and technical vulnerabilities across multiple provisions of the ITA.

On the governance plane, ADC was dependent on the cash flow provided by Seawind Corp. under the development agreement, which reimbursed ADC's expenses net of the refundable SR&ED tax credits it received, credits that ADC was in turn required to remit to Seawind Corp.; ADC had nominal share capital, operated at a deficit, and recorded the full amount of the credits on its balance sheets without showing the offsetting liability to Seawind Corp. Because Mr. Silva and Seawind Corp. controlled the sole source of working capital and commercial revenue, notes to some of ADC's financial statements highlighted its economic dependence on Seawind Corp., and when Seawind Corp. ceased providing financing, ADC ceased operations. The Federal Court of Appeal treated this near-total economic dependence as a very relevant factor in finding non-arm's length dealings, while holding that such financial and operational dependence could not by itself ground de facto control under subsection 256(5.1) as interpreted in McGillivray Restaurant.

Furthermore, on the expenditure qualification plane under subsections 37(1) and 127(9) of the ITA, qualified SR&ED expenditures eligible for ITCs must be reduced by any "government assistance," "non-government assistance," or "contract payment" that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive. While payments received from a non-resident customer for R&D performed on its behalf generally do not constitute a "contract payment" under subsection 127(9) provided the foreign payor is not carrying on business in Canada or claiming a Canadian tax deduction, structuring foreign inflows as non-arm's length subsidies, expense reimbursements, or on-demand advances while simultaneously claiming CCPC status creates an irreconcilable statutory contradiction. By relying on Mr. Silva's direct financial backing and captive R&D mandate while claiming that ADC was an independent, Canadian-controlled entity, ADC trapped itself: the very development agreement that sustained its R&D operations was the legally enforceable arrangement through which Mr. Silva and Seawind Corp. held influence amounting to control in fact, and the non-arm's length character of the relationship deprived ADC of the supply-agreement exception.
Failure 4: Technical and Documentation Risks in Aircraft Certification vs. Experimental Development

Although the dispositive threshold issue in 2017 TCC 39 and 2018 FCA 67 centred on ADC's corporate status as a CCPC rather than a line-by-line reassessment of its aeronautical engineering activities, the factual background of the dispute—completing the prototyping and certification of the Seawind aircraft from a hangar in St-Jean-sur-Richelieu, Quebec—illustrates a critical technical boundary in Canadian SR&ED law.

Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, a claimant must establish that its activities constitute a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis to achieve a technological advancement through the resolution of technological uncertainty. In the aerospace industry, activities aimed strictly at demonstrating compliance with Transport Canada or foreign aviation airworthiness regulations—routine certification testing of an established airframe design—do not qualify as experimental development unless the testing uncovers an underlying technological uncertainty that cannot be resolved through standard engineering practice. For example, whereas third-party aerospace patents unrelated to ADC (which, under its development agreement, owned none of the intellectual property arising from its work, all such rights belonging to Mr. Silva and Seawind Corp.) describe complex acoustic attenuation panels, micro-perforated polymeric liners, and one-piece monocoque graphite/epoxy engine inlet barrels requiring novel co-curing methodologies, airworthiness flight certification of an existing aircraft configuration requires rigorous technical segregation. When a single-purpose corporation like ADC is organized around a certification mandate ("attempting to have aircraft certified"), any failure to maintain contemporaneous documentation isolating genuine technological uncertainties and structured hypothesis-driven experimentation from routine regulatory compliance testing exposes the technical claim to disallowance, while the loss of CCPC status strips the corporation of enhanced cash refundability for each affected taxation year.
Failure 5: Procedural Objection to the Unpleaded Arm's Length Issue

Before the Tax Court of Canada, the initial evidentiary onus rests on the taxpayer to demolish the Minister's assumptions of fact pleaded in the Reply to the Notice of Appeal. In Aeronautic Development Corporation, ADC argued on appeal that it was not open to the Tax Court to consider whether ADC was dealing at arm's length with Mr. Silva and Seawind Corp., because the Minister's Reply had not specifically pleaded that position.

The Federal Court of Appeal rejected this objection without relying on subsection 152(9) of the ITA: the pleading rules exist to ensure fairness so that a taxpayer is not unfairly taken by surprise (as in Heron Bay Investments Ltd. v. Canada, 2010 FCA 203, and Pedwell v. Canada, [2000] 4 F.C. 616, where reliance on unpleaded provisions was found improper), but here ADC's own reliance on the exception in subsection 256(5.1) put the arm's length issue into play, ADC's counsel conceded he had anticipated the need to address it, and he made submissions on it in response to the Tax Court judge's questions without objection. Because ADC was not taken by surprise and the arm's length issue formed part of its own defence to the Crown's claim of de facto control, any grounds to object were waived by counsel's submissions, and its procedural objection failed.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and legal requirement examined in Aeronautic Development Corporation v. Her Majesty the Queen (2017 TCC 39, aff'd 2018 FCA 67) against the taxpayer's specific factual and legal failures and the governing judicial standard of proof in Canada.

headers: Taxpayer's Specific Failure in Aeronautic Development Corp.
Judicial Standard of Proof & Evidentiary Threshold

cells: Qualification as a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC)

ADC claimed CCPC status based on de jure voting share ownership by one employee and Canadian corporations controlled by three employees (Seawind Corp. retaining 46% of the voting common shares), ignoring the overarching de facto control exercised by the non-resident founder, Mr. Silva, through Seawind Corp.

The taxpayer must prove on a balance of probabilities that it is a private Canadian corporation not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-residents or public corporations throughout the entire taxation year.
Absence of Non-Resident De Facto Control (Control in Fact)
ITA s. 256(5.1) (and s. 256(5.11) post-March 21, 2017); McGillivray Restaurant Ltd. v. The Queen, 2016 FCA 99

The development agreement dictated by Mr. Silva was a legally enforceable (supply) arrangement giving Seawind Corp. and Mr. Silva influence that, if exercised, would result in control in fact of ADC, and the exception in s. 256(5.1) was unavailable because ADC was not dealing at arm's length with them.

Under s. 256(5.1) (pre-2017), the Court examines whether a non-resident has a legally enforceable right and ability to change the board of directors or influence the shareholders who have that right. Post-2017 (s. 256(5.11)), the Court must consider all operational, economic, and commercial factors.
Factual Arm's Length Dealings Between ADC and the Non-Resident Controllers (Seawind Corp. and Mr. Silva)

Mr. Silva dictated the terms of the development agreement and unilaterally decided the 5% mark-up would not be paid; ADC did not renegotiate the agreement after its initial 15-month term despite operating at a deficit, and occupied a hangar leased by another Silva-controlled corporation rent-free and without a lease.

Question of fact requiring objective documentary and testimonial proof of independent bargaining, separate economic risk and reward, and the absence of a single directing mind or overbearing influence.
Entitlement to Enhanced 35% Refundable SR&ED Investment Tax Credits
ITA s. 127(9), s. 127(10.1), s. 127.1(1)
Because ADC was disqualified as a CCPC for its 2009–2011 taxation years, its entitlement to the enhanced 35% ITC rate and cash refundability under s. 127.1 collapsed entirely.

Strict statutory compliance: CCPC status is a binary condition precedent. Failure to maintain CCPC status throughout the taxation year eliminates access to the 35% rate and federal ITC refundability for that taxation year.
Distinction Between Certification Testing and Eligible SR&ED Experimental Development
ITA s. 248(1), s. 37(1)

Operating as a single-asset certification vehicle for the Seawind aircraft exposed ADC to the risk that routine regulatory airworthiness testing would be conflated with eligible experimental development.
Contemporaneous technical documentation proving technological uncertainty, explicit hypothesis formulation, a structured process of experimentation, and resulting technological advancement.
Objection to Issues Not Specifically Pleaded in the Minister's Reply
Pleading fairness principles (Heron Bay Investments Ltd. v. Canada, 2010 FCA 203; Pedwell v. Canada, [2000] 4 F.C. 616); ITA s. 256(5.1) exception

ADC argued on appeal that the Tax Court could not consider the arm's length issue because the Minister had not pleaded it, although its own reliance on the s. 256(5.1) exception put that issue in play and its counsel addressed it at trial without objection.

Pleading rules protect taxpayers against unfair surprise; no breach of procedural fairness arises where the taxpayer was alive to the issue, it formed part of its own defence, and any objection was waived by making submissions on the point.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the judicial holdings of Aeronautic Development Corporation v. Her Majesty the Queen (2017 TCC 39, aff'd 2018 FCA 67) into actionable legal and technical tax architecture, the following two applied industry case studies demonstrate how Canadian corporations facing identical structural, contractual, and evidentiary pitfalls can proactively restructure their governance, commercial agreements, and SR&ED documentation to withstand CRA audit and Tax Court of Canada scrutiny.
Case Study 1: Cross-Border Aerospace Acoustic Nacelle and Avionics R&D Venture
Baseline Scenario and Identified Legal Pitfalls

Boreal AeroStructures Inc. ("Boreal") is an aerospace engineering corporation incorporated in Canada and headquartered in Montreal, Quebec. Boreal was formed to develop a novel one-piece monocoque composite engine inlet acoustic barrel and micro-perforated polymeric liner designed to attenuate dominant turbo-fan blade-passage frequencies while integrating an autonomous de-icing leading-edge ring. The core intellectual property concept originated with Zephyr Propulsion LLC ("Zephyr"), a United States corporation wholly owned by Dr. Marcus Vance, a non-resident of Canada. To claim the 35% federal refundable SR&ED ITC on its Quebec engineering operations, Zephyr subscribed for 100% of Boreal's Class B non-voting preferred shares for $2,500,000 USD, while Boreal issued 60% of its Class A common voting shares to two Canadian aeronautical engineers employed by Boreal for a total subscription price of $60 CAD ($30 CAD each), with Zephyr holding the remaining 40% of the Class A common voting shares.

Under an informal side agreement and a captive R&D Services Agreement, the two Canadian engineers agreed to elect Dr. Vance's nominee as the sole director of Boreal and to transfer their Class A shares back to Zephyr for $60 CAD upon demand. Boreal performs 100% of its engineering and NRC wind-tunnel certification testing exclusively for Zephyr on a cost-plus-5% reimbursement basis, with Zephyr retaining all background and foreground intellectual property. Meanwhile, Boreal's internal engineering logs consist solely of Transport Canada airworthiness certification pass/fail test sheets without isolating the underlying composite curing or acoustic impedance uncertainties.

This baseline structure replicates—and, in its share-capital features, goes beyond—the vulnerabilities that caused the disallowance in Aeronautic Development Corporation (2017 TCC 39, aff'd 2018 FCA 67). Under subsections 125(7), 256(5.1), and 256(5.11) of the ITA, Dr. Vance and Zephyr hold de facto control over Boreal because the Canadian voting shareholders hold nominal $30 shares without genuine economic risk, are subject to an on-demand repurchase arrangement, and submit to Dr. Vance's influence in electing the board of directors. Furthermore, the Canadian engineers fail the factual arm's length test under paragraph 251(1)(c) because they act in concert with Dr. Vance as accommodation shareholders without separate economic interests. Finally, because Boreal operates as a captive certification contractor whose engineering records only track regulatory compliance milestones rather than a structured process of experimentation addressing technological uncertainty, the technical claim itself is vulnerable to disallowance under subsection 248(1).
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Plan
Step 1: Corporate Governance and Share Capital Restructuring

To establish unimpeachable CCPC status under subsection 125(7) and eliminate non-resident de facto control (s. 256(5.1) and s. 256(5.11)) as well as factual non-arm's length dealings (s. 251(1)(c)), Boreal must execute a comprehensive corporate reorganization prior to the commencement of the taxation year. First, Boreal must eliminate the nominal $60 accommodation share structure by recruiting an independent Canadian resident angel syndicate, a Canadian aerospace venture fund (itself a CCPC or partnership of Canadian residents), or independent Canadian resident co-founders who invest substantive, at-risk capital (for example, $750,000 CAD) at fair market value to acquire 55% of the common voting and fully participating equity shares of Boreal, while Zephyr holds 45% of the common voting shares alongside non-voting, non-participating preferred shares carrying a fixed, non-cumulative dividend without redemption-on-demand rights.

Second, Boreal must rescind all call options, demand repurchase rights, voting trusts, or side letters that permit Zephyr or Dr. Vance to acquire the Canadian shareholders' voting shares or dictate their voting behaviour. In addition to preventing de facto control under subsection 256(5.1), extinguishing contingent acquisition rights avoids triggering paragraph 251(5)(b) of the ITA, which otherwise deems a non-resident who holds a contractual right to acquire shares or control voting rights to occupy the same position as if the non-resident owned the shares currently. Third, the shareholders must execute a Unanimous Shareholder Agreement (USA) that vests majority board appointment rights strictly in the Canadian resident majority voting shareholders—such as a three-person board comprising two independent Canadian resident directors elected exclusively by the Canadian shareholders and one director nominated by Zephyr. The USA must restrict Zephyr to standard minority protective vetoes over fundamental corporate changes and explicitly deny Zephyr any veto power over annual R&D budgets, executive hiring or termination, customer diversification, or operational management, thereby satisfying both the McGillivray Restaurant legal enforceability test (s. 256(5.1)) and the broader multi-factor operational test under subsection 256(5.11).
Step 2: Commercial, Financing, and Intellectual Property Contract Restructuring

To dismantle the single-client captive subcontractor profile that undermined ADC in 2017 TCC 39, Boreal must restructure its commercial and intellectual property contracts with Zephyr so that Boreal operates as an autonomous, risk-bearing Canadian enterprise. Boreal should terminate the cost-plus-5% R&D Services Agreement and replace it with an arm's length Background IP License and Commercial Offtake Agreement. Under this revised contractual architecture, Boreal acquires an exclusive field-of-use license to Zephyr's background acoustic liner patents in exchange for a commercial royalty on future product sales, while Boreal retains 100% legal and beneficial ownership of all foreground Canadian intellectual property developed during its SR&ED projects in Quebec.

Simultaneously, any financing provided by Zephyr must be structured as fixed-term, non-convertible subordinated debt with commercial maturity dates (such as five-year term notes with standard financial covenants and no demand-repayment feature) or non-voting preferred shares without retraction rights. Removing on-demand repayment mechanisms prevents the non-resident from threatening immediate insolvency to coerce the Canadian directors or shareholders. Furthermore, Boreal's board must enact a multi-client commercialization mandate directing management to market and license its acoustic nacelle liner technology to third-party Canadian and international aircraft original equipment manufacturers, establishing independent commercial viability outside of Zephyr.
Step 3: Technical Documentation and Structured Experimentation Tracking

To insulate the underlying engineering claim from CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) challenges regarding aircraft certification testing under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, Boreal must implement dual-track project accounting in its enterprise resource planning and time-tracking systems. Engineering hours and NRC facility fees expended on standard Transport Canada airworthiness compliance tests for frozen designs must be segregated and coded to non-SR&ED commercial engineering accounts.

Conversely, whenever an acoustic attenuation or composite structural failure occurs during testing that cannot be resolved through standard aeronautical engineering practice—for instance, when co-curing the graphite/epoxy inner perforate face skin and honeycomb core over a 360-degree monocoque barrel causes resin migration that blocks the micro-perforated porous layer and degrades acoustic impedance—Boreal must open a dedicated SR&ED Technical Dossier. Within that dossier, project engineers must contemporaneously record the specific technological uncertainty by quantifying why existing composite layup and autoclave curing models cannot simultaneously achieve zero-splice structural integrity and uniform acoustic porosity across a 360-degree cylindrical geometry. Engineers must then document explicit, testable hypotheses linking release-layer viscosity, curing pressure gradients, and pin-alignment tolerances to acoustic attenuation performance, followed by systematic experimental logs detailing iterative fabrication runs, ultrasonic porosity measurements, acoustic impedance tube testing, and finite element analysis correlations. Finally, each technical dossier must articulate the resulting technological advancement in composite materials processing, independent of whether a specific prototype passes regulatory airworthiness certification.
Case Study 2: Biopharmaceutical Microfluidic Assay Spin-Out with Foreign Strategic Backing
Baseline Scenario and Identified Legal Pitfalls

Vanguard BioDiagnostics Ltd. ("Vanguard") is an Ontario-incorporated biotechnology corporation developing an automated microfluidic point-of-care immunoassay cartridge capable of multiplexing low-abundance oncology biomarkers from whole blood without centrifugation. Vanguard was spun out of a European diagnostics conglomerate, EuroMed AG, a non-resident corporation headquartered in Zurich, Switzerland. To enable Vanguard to claim the 35% federal refundable SR&ED ITC on $2,800,000 of annual Canadian laboratory salaries and consumables, EuroMed AG structured Vanguard's share capital such that EuroMed AG holds 49% of Vanguard's common voting shares, while the remaining 51% of Vanguard's common voting shares are held by Vanguard's Chief Scientific Officer (CSO), Dr. Elena Rostova, a Canadian citizen residing in Toronto.

Dr. Rostova acquired her 51% voting block through an interest-free, non-recourse promissory note issued by EuroMed AG, secured solely by a pledge of the shares. Under the Pledge and Financing Agreement, EuroMed AG can call the promissory note at any time upon 15 days' written notice; if Dr. Rostova does not remit $1,500,000 in cash within 15 days, her 51% voting shares are automatically forfeited to EuroMed AG. In addition, Dr. Rostova remains a paid scientific consultant to EuroMed AG under a separate consulting contract that generates 65% of her personal annual income. In the Toronto laboratory, Vanguard's scientists perform thousands of assay screening runs, recording raw fluorescence outputs in unindexed spreadsheets without documenting the underlying biochemical hypotheses or distinguishing routine quality-control validation from experimental development.

Vanguard is acutely exposed to reassessment and total disallowance of its refundable ITCs under the principles of Aeronautic Development Corporation (2017 TCC 39, aff'd 2018 FCA 67). EuroMed AG possesses de facto control under subsections 256(5.1) and 256(5.11) because the 15-day demand non-recourse promissory note and share pledge give EuroMed AG the immediate legal and economic ability to strip Dr. Rostova of her 51% voting shares or compel her to vote in accordance with EuroMed AG's directives in electing the board of directors. Furthermore, Dr. Rostova's dependence on EuroMed AG for 65% of her personal income and her non-recourse financing arrangement establish factual non-arm's length dealings under paragraph 251(1)(c). Compounding these corporate control defects, the absence of contemporaneous hypothesis and experimentation records violates the technical substantiation standards required under subsection 248(1).
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Plan
Step 1: Restructuring Shareholder Financing, Independence, and Control

To cure the de facto control and non-arm's length defects identified in 2017 TCC 39 and 2018 FCA 67, Vanguard must completely sever the financial and legal levers connecting Dr. Rostova's voting shares to EuroMed AG. Vanguard and its shareholders must immediately extinguish the EuroMed AG non-recourse promissory note and release the share pledge over Dr. Rostova's voting shares. Because Dr. Rostova cannot personally fund a $1,500,000 subscription on a commercial basis, Vanguard should syndicate the majority Canadian voting equity (for example, 58% of the voting shares) among Dr. Rostova—investing independent personal funds on a full-recourse, fair-market-value basis—and arm's length Canadian life-sciences venture capital funds or Canadian resident angel investors, thereby reducing EuroMed AG to a true minority shareholder (42% voting equity) with zero contingent rights under paragraph 251(5)(b) to acquire additional voting shares.

Concurrently, Dr. Rostova must terminate her external consulting agreement with EuroMed AG so that she is compensated exclusively by Vanguard under a market-rate employment agreement approved by an independent compensation committee of Vanguard's Canadian-majority board of directors, eliminating EuroMed AG's personal economic leverage over her. Vanguard must also reconstitute its board of directors into a five-member board comprising Dr. Rostova, two independent Canadian resident directors appointed by the Canadian venture syndicate, and two directors nominated by EuroMed AG. Corporate counsel must maintain detailed, contemporaneous minute books demonstrating that the Canadian-majority board independently debates, modifies, and approves annual R&D budgets, clinical trial designs, and financing term sheets, providing objective documentary proof to demolish any Ministerial assumption of non-resident de facto control pleaded in the Minister's Reply at the Tax Court stage.
Step 2: Commercial Contracting and R&D Risk Allocation

To ensure that EuroMed AG's commercial relationship with Vanguard neither triggers de facto operational control under subsection 256(5.11) nor reduces Vanguard's qualified SR&ED expenditure pool under subsection 127(9), Vanguard must structure its commercial arrangements so that it bears full technical and financial risk for its Canadian R&D program. Rather than EuroMed AG reimbursing Vanguard's R&D expenditures as non-government assistance, EuroMed AG's capital infusion must be confined to its minority equity subscription, coupled with an arm's length Commercial Distribution Agreement granting EuroMed AG exclusive European distribution rights for fully commercialized microfluidic cartridges at arm's length transfer prices, while Vanguard retains North American and rest-of-world commercialization rights. Additionally, Vanguard must contract directly with Canadian university hospital networks and independent microfluidic foundries so that its supply chain, clinical validation, and laboratory infrastructure operate autonomously from EuroMed AG.
Step 3: Restructuring Laboratory Documentation and Experimentation Tracking

To transform Vanguard's unindexed assay screening spreadsheets into audit-proof SR&ED documentation satisfying subsection 248(1) of the ITA, Vanguard must replace ad-hoc spreadsheets with a validated Electronic Laboratory Notebook (ELN) system configured around the statutory criteria of technological uncertainty, hypothesis formulation, systematic experimentation, and technological advancement. Vanguard's R&D directors must group individual experimental runs into defined SR&ED projects centred on system-level technological uncertainties—such as resolving non-specific protein adsorption on cyclic olefin copolymer micro-channels when modulating electro-osmotic flow velocities in whole blood—while excluding routine quality-control lot validation.

Prior to executing each experimental series, principal investigators must record in the ELN the specific biochemical or fluid-dynamic hypothesis being tested, the independent variables manipulated (such as surfactant surface-grafting density, channel aspect ratio, and buffer ionic strength), the quantitative experimental observations and statistical variance analysis, and the scientific conclusion explaining why the hypothesis was confirmed, refuted, or modified for the subsequent experimental iteration. By linking laboratory personnel timecards bi-weekly to specific ELN experiment identifiers, Vanguard establishes an unbroken, contemporaneous evidentiary chain connecting its technological uncertainties directly to its claimed SR&ED salary and material expenditures.
5. Synthesis and Strategic Conclusions for Canadian SR&ED Advisors

The rulings of the Tax Court of Canada (2017 TCC 39) and the Federal Court of Appeal (2018 FCA 67), reinforced by the Supreme Court of Canada's dismissal of leave to appeal with costs on March 7, 2019 (Docket 38132), establish that Canadian courts will conduct a rigorous, substance-oriented inquiry into the legal arrangements binding a corporation to a non-resident, arm's length dealings, and de facto control whenever a corporation with significant non-resident involvement claims enhanced refundable CCPC SR&ED tax credits. De jure voting structures in which Canadian residents hold a majority of voting shares while a non-resident principal retains, through legally enforceable agreements and non-arm's length dealings with the corporation, influence that if exercised would result in control in fact will not secure CCPC status under subsections 125(7) and 256(5.1) and paragraph 251(1)(c) of the Income Tax Act, even though, for taxation years beginning before March 22, 2017, merely operational or economic influence was held insufficient on its own. Moreover, following the enactment of subsection 256(5.11), the judicial lens has widened even further to encompass the totality of operational, contractual, and commercial dependencies. Consequently, Canadian tax counsel and technical SR&ED advisors must integrate corporate governance engineering, arm's length capitalization, commercial contract risk allocation, and contemporaneous scientific documentation into a unified compliance architecture prior to the start of each taxation year.

outcome: Appeal dismissed; FCA affirmed TCC's ruling that the corporation was not a CCPC and was ineligible for enhanced SR&ED rates.
